questions.prompt: For a parallel-plate (MIM) capacitor with area \(A\), dielectric thickness \(t\) and permittivity \(\varepsilon\), the capacitance is
options: \(C=\dfrac{\varepsilon t}{A}\)
\(C=\dfrac{At}{\varepsilon}\)
\(C=\varepsilon At\)
\(C=\dfrac{\varepsilon A}{t}\)
questions.explanation: The field is \(E=V/t\) (Eq. 4.20), Gauss gives \(Q=\varepsilon EA\) (Eq. 4.21), so \(Q=\dfrac{\varepsilon A}{t}V\) (Eq. 4.22). A bigger area or a thinner dielectric gives more capacitance.

questions.prompt: What is the oxide capacitance per area of a 20 nm SiO₂ layer (\(\varepsilon_{ox}=3.45\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{F/cm}\)), in \(\mathrm{fF/\mu m^2}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(C_{ox}=\dfrac{\varepsilon_{ox}}{t_{ox}}=\dfrac{3.45\times10^{-13}}{2\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{cm}}=1.73\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{F/cm^2}=173\ \mathrm{nF/cm^2}\).
Since \(1\ \mathrm{cm^2}=10^8\ \mu\mathrm{m^2}\): \(1.73\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{F}/10^8=1.727\ \mathrm{fF/\mu m^2}\).
Reader note: the Sec. 7.6.4 example writes this result as '172.5 nF'; the unit should be nF/cm².

questions.prompt: Why are the charges on the two plates of a capacitor equal and opposite?
options: Because the plates have the same area
Because the battery forces it, independent of electrostatics
The insulator is charge-free, so the field is uniform across it; by Gauss's law, the field lines leaving the top plate must all end on the bottom plate
They aren't; the top plate always has more charge
questions.explanation: Reader Fig. 4.12: with \(\rho=0\) between the plates, \(E\) is constant, and Gauss's law at each plate gives \(+Q\) and \(-Q\) of the same size.

questions.prompt: Design a 1 pF MIM capacitor with a 30 nm SiO₂ dielectric. What plate area is needed, in \(\mu\mathrm{m^2}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(A=\dfrac{Ct}{\varepsilon_{ox}}=\dfrac{10^{-12}\times3\times10^{-6}}{3.453\times10^{-13}}=8.69\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{cm^2}=868.8\ \mu\mathrm{m^2}\) (about \(29.5\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) on a side).
Capacitors are expensive in chip area.

questions.prompt: That capacitor (30 nm dielectric) has 3.3 V across it. What is the field in the dielectric, in MV/cm?
questions.explanation: \(E=V/t=3.3/(3\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{cm})=1.1\times10^6\ \mathrm{V/cm}=1.1\ \mathrm{MV/cm}\), comfortably below the ~10 MV/cm breakdown of SiO₂.

questions.prompt: The dielectric thickness of a MIM capacitor is halved, at the same applied voltage. What happens?
options: \(C\) doubles and the field is unchanged
\(C\) doubles and the field in the dielectric doubles
\(C\) halves and the field doubles
\(C\) is unchanged and the field doubles
questions.explanation: \(C=\varepsilon A/t\) doubles. \(E=V/t\) also doubles, which is why thin dielectrics give dense capacitors but limit the maximum voltage (breakdown).

questions.prompt: A MIM capacitor's bottom plate has a large parasitic capacitance to the substrate. One terminal connects to a sensitive high-impedance node, the other to a low-impedance driven node. How should you connect it?
options: Bottom plate to the low-impedance node, top plate to the sensitive node
Bottom plate to the sensitive node
It doesn't matter; the capacitor is symmetric
Connect both plates to the sensitive node
questions.explanation: The bottom-plate parasitic (reader Sec. 4.5.1) loads whatever node the bottom plate touches. On a driven (low-impedance) node it does little harm; on a high-impedance node it adds capacitance and couples substrate noise. The physical structure is NOT symmetric.

questions.prompt: A capacitor dielectric is a stack: 10 nm of SiO₂ (\(3.9\varepsilon_0\)) on 10 nm of a high-k film (\(7.8\varepsilon_0\)). What is the capacitance per area, in \(\mathrm{fF/\mu m^2}\)?
questions.explanation:
With no charge at the internal interface, \(D=\varepsilon E\) is the same in both layers, so the voltages add: \(V=\sigma\left(\dfrac{t_1}{\varepsilon_1}+\dfrac{t_2}{\varepsilon_2}\right)\). That's two capacitors in series.
\(\dfrac{C}{A}=\dfrac{1}{t_1/\varepsilon_1+t_2/\varepsilon_2}\): the high-k layer acts like 5 nm of SiO₂, so it's like a 15 nm oxide: \(\dfrac{3.453\times10^{-13}}{1.5\times10^{-6}}=2.302\ \mathrm{fF/\mu m^2}\).
Common mistake: averaging the permittivities (\(5.85\varepsilon_0\) over 20 nm gives 2.59 fF/µm²).

questions.prompt: For an ideal capacitor with perfect metal plates, where does the charge reside?
options: Uniformly throughout the plate thickness
Spread uniformly through the dielectric
At the outer surfaces facing away from the dielectric
At the plate surfaces facing the dielectric (a thin sheet, like a delta function), with zero field inside the metal
questions.explanation: The field inside an ideal conductor is zero, so by Gauss's law there is no net charge inside the metal; it sits at the surface facing the other plate (reader Fig. 4.13(b)). Because the charge stays at a fixed separation \(t\), \(Q=CV\) is linear. When charge penetrates into the plates (as in semiconductors), that changes.

questions.prompt: Preview of small-signal capacitance. A linear 1 pF capacitor is biased at 2.0 V, and the voltage rises to 2.1 V. How much extra charge flows onto it, in pC?
questions.explanation: \(\Delta Q=C\,\Delta V=1\ \mathrm{pF}\times0.1\ \mathrm{V}=0.1\ \mathrm{pC}\). For a linear capacitor \(\Delta Q/\Delta V=Q/V=C\) at every bias. The next skill meets capacitors where \(dQ/dV\) depends on the bias.
questions.figure_alt: A straight-line Q-V plot with a bias point at 2 V.

questions.prompt: Preview of junction capacitance. A depleted silicon layer \(0.2\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) thick behaves like a parallel-plate dielectric (\(\varepsilon_s=11.7\varepsilon_0\)). What capacitance per area would it have, in \(\mathrm{fF/\mu m^2}\)?
questions.explanation:
\(C/A=\varepsilon_s/X=\dfrac{1.036\times10^{-12}}{2\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}}=5.18\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{F/cm^2}=0.518\ \mathrm{fF/\mu m^2}\).
The PN-junction capacitance has exactly this form, \(\varepsilon_s/X_{dep}\), except that \(X_{dep}\) changes with bias.

questions.prompt: Preview of non-linear capacitors. Suppose a 'plate' isn't an ideal metal, so its charge spreads into a layer whose thickness grows with the applied voltage. What happens to the Q–V curve?
options: It stays linear, \(Q=CV\)
The capacitance becomes zero
It becomes non-linear: the effective plate separation changes with \(V\), so \(Q/V\) and \(dQ/dV\) depend on bias
The charges on the two plates become unequal
questions.explanation: \(C=\varepsilon A/t\) assumes the charges sit at a fixed separation. If the charge layer thickens with \(V\), the charge centroid moves and the effective \(t\) changes, so \(Q(V)\) bends (reader Fig. 4.14–4.15). Charge neutrality still holds.
